   Pollock; sustainable education; third culture kids
ID 3RD-CULTURE KIDS
AB This study investigates effects of shifting educational systems on Third Culture Kids (TCKs), emphasizing the impact of a nomadic lifestyle on learning, identity, and personal development. It addresses key gaps in research on TCKs' educational and emotional experiences, highlighting both strengths and challenges of a peripatetic upbringing. Using an autoethnographic approach, along with secondary data, this study integrates personal lived experience with existing literature to examine the effects of mobility on education and identity.    School Principals
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE barriers to education; Nuh District; right to education; School
   Development Plan; School Management Committee
AB The School Management Committees (SMCs) are established under the Right to Education Act, 2009. The main objective of this paper is to know the perceptions of school heads regarding the working of SMCs in government elementary schools in an educationally backward district (Nuh) in the State of Haryana. The researchers applied an interview questionnaire technique to collect the data from School heads. The questions were both openended and closed-ended. The schools were selected systematically and the collected data is analysed both quantitatively and qualitatively. The observational data disclosed corruption, high absenteeism among students, cultural obstacles to education, lack of women's participation in school governance and unequal distribution of resources in the educational blocks. This paper contributes to readers knowing more about hindrances to educational access in Nuh District and the effectiveness of SMCs. Based on the findings, this research recommends providing an awareness campaign to the parents and holding training programs for SMC members.

TI Teaching for Social Justice: Rethinking the Educator's Role in Equity
   and Inclusion
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE conceptions; challenges social justice teaching; pedagogy; practices
ID CHALLENGES; CLASSROOMS
AB Social justice teaching is an educational approach that confronts systemic inequities, encourages students to become change agents, and establishes equitable learning environments. The current study explored teacher educators' practices to explore how social justice teaching is implemented in higher education classrooms. The study aimed to understand the ideas, pedagogical approaches, and difficulties of incorporating social justice values in classroom settings. The main research objectives were (i) how teacher educators understand social justice, (ii) how they put social justice into practice in a higher education setting, and (iii) what obstacles they encounter while putting social justice into practice. To gather qualitative data, 32 semi-structured interviews with teachers were conducted. NVivo 12 and thematic analysis were used to evaluate the qualitative data, while descriptive statistics (SPSS, 21) were used to analyze quantitative data. The data were additionally triangulated with the responses of the students (n=527). The data revealed teacher educators' experience in implementing the social justice values of democracy, diversity, and equity in their classrooms. They highlighted that education is a potent agent for social advancement rather than being neutral. The movement towards a future characterized by justice, equity, and opportunity for all can be spearheaded by educators and students working together.

TI Reimagining Dignified Inclusive Higher Education: System-Level
   Strategies of a South African University
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE case study; diversity; inclusion; intergroup contact; macropsychology;
   situational analysis
ID INTERGROUP CONTACT; DIGNITY
AB This case study draws from the macro psychology perspective and intergroup contact theory to identify the system-level strategies employed by the management of a historically White South African University to promote intergroup contact and inclusion between racially and ethnically diverse students. Different sources of data were collected, including N=8 openended interviews with purposively selected managers and representatives who played key roles in diversity management and transformation, website documents, shared organizational documents, visual materials (e.g., photos), and the main researcher's field notes. Data analysis followed the methodology of situational analysis, which is an extension of Grounded Theory. The strategies identified displayed dynamic interrelationships across the different levels, namely, system-level (macro level), group-relational (meso level), and intra-individual (micro level). Overall, system-level intergroup contact practices between racially and ethnically diverse groups are the most effective when deliberate, value-driven, and supported by all the departments within the institution. Institutional practices that allocate resources to encourage and support student-led initiatives serve to advance the representation and empowerment of marginalized outgroups. In turn, this allows for active engagement between students and management to be more centered on the students' needs to improve the campus culture. This study endeavors to provide learning points from a post-conflict South African context that remains relatively underexplored in the reimagining of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) from a macro level and intergroup contact perspective. South Africa can offer valuable insights to the Global North regarding best management practices of DEI focused on promoting intercultural contact and social inclusion.

TI Qualified by Different Standards: Challenging Historical Narratives in
   Ontario's Teacher Education
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Keywords : Canada; human capital theory; initial teacher education;
   Ontario; teachers' colleges
ID NURSING-EDUCATION; CANADA; UNIVERSITY; SCHOOLS
AB Initial Teacher Education (ITE) is a highly contested professional training field. Critics question whether teachers produced by teacher education programs have the knowledge, aptitudes and skills to teach and whether their students achieve to academic, attitudinal, and employment outcomes expected of them. For Ontario, Canada in the 1960s and 1970s, ITE programs were too short and too crammed to provide prospective teachers with practical skills, subject matter content, and theoretical knowledge for a changing society. One approach to enhance elementary teacher training was transferring responsibility to universities. While a conceptually straightforward proposition, transitioning a one-year teacher training scheme to a four-year undergraduate and professional program posed difficult questions if there were enough qualified people to teach in these programs and if the inclusion of teacher education undermined the purpose and value of university education. In this paper, university leaders' claim that Ontario's teachers' college masters were not qualified for university positions was tested. Academic qualifications of teachers' college were compared to instructors to faculty at two institutional dyads, St. Catharines Teachers' College/Brock University and Windsor Teachers' College/University of Windsor during institutional mergers, showing that teachers' college staff academic qualifications were equivalent to those of academic appointments in selected professional programs. The discussion on value and professionalism resonates with contemporary debates on the quality of teacher education and similar transfers of teacher training to university-affiliated programs in other nations.

TI From Equity to Containment? A Critical Analysis of Compensatory
   Education in Portugal
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational inequality; compensatory education; social mobility; school
   autonomy; teip; vocational education
ID TITLE I; LEADERSHIP; SCHOOLS
AB This article assesses the performance differences (2001/02-2015/16) among schools that integrate Portugal's main compensatory education programme-Territ & oacute;rios Educativos de Interven & ccedil;& atilde;o Priorit & aacute;ria (TEIP). Drawing on a mixed-methods approach, the study combines a longitudinal analysis of quantitative educational data with semi-structured interviews conducted with headteachers and TEIP coordinators in 6 secondary schools selected for their contrasting trajectories. Although TEIP schools benefit from greater autonomy and additional human and material resources-factors often cited as enabling pedagogical innovation and community engagement-, the evidence indicates that school-level outcomes are associated with a) how autonomy and resources are translated into internal monitoring and organisational routines; b) the expansion of vocational education, which in some contexts coincides with reduced exam intensity and more limited routes into higher education; and c) structural inequalities and reputational dynamics that shape intake composition and partnerships. The analysis suggests that TEIP can align with broader changes in the Portuguese educational context; however, an equity-oriented discourse may at times coincide with patterns of social segregation, channelling disadvantaged populations toward less socially prestigious labour-market opportunities. Accordingly, the results are interpreted as associational, not causal, and we note a key data limitation: the absence of comparable school-level indicators on higher-education transitions and long-term employment outcomes. Overall, the study is consistent with the hypothesis that compensatory education, while well-intentioned, may inadvertently reproduce social hierarchies unless accompanied by redistributive, recognition and representation policies that mitigate structural inequalities. These findings raise critical questions about TEIP's transformative potential for upward mobility and social inclusion.

TI Cursed by Accuracy: Exploring Decolonial Practices in Undoing the Native
   Speaker Spell
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE accuracy; decolonial pedagogy; English as a foreign language; English
   learners; Japanese native-speakerism
ID LANGUAGE; IDEOLOGIES; ENGLISH
AB Focusing on one Japanese English learner Mami (pseudonym), whose pursuit of grammatical accuracy reflects Japanese English education which emphasizes morphosyntactic precision, this case study examines how raciolinguistic ideologies manifest in the language learning experiences of Japanese university students majoring in English. Mami's experiences are contrasted with two other students in her class, those of Hayao and Ryota (pseudonyms), who have lived in non-English dominant countries. Drawing on questionnaires, writing samples, and a focus-group interview, the analysis shows how Mami's accuracy anxiety functions not simply as a cognitive or pedagogical concern but as an ontological and raciolinguistic effect, shaped by colonial histories of linguistic legitimacy, reinforced by Japanese education. Situated within scholarship on native-speakerism, English imperialism, decolonial pedagogy and raciolinguistics, the paper argues that learning environments outside the Anglophone "centre" can unsettle the association between English mastery and whiteness. By linking grammatical accuracy to colonial affect, this paper extends raciolinguistic inquiry and calls for a decolonial reorientation of English learning in Japan, one that values pluriversal encounters over proximity to so-called native speakers.

TI A Machine Learning Approach to Predict Technology Integration Among
   Mathematics Teacher Educators
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE decision tree model; mathematics education; predictive analysis; teacher
   proficiency; technology integration
ID SELF-EFFICACY; ACCEPTANCE MODEL; USER ACCEPTANCE; UNIFIED THEORY;
   ADOPTION; BELIEFS; LOAD; ICT
AB This study aims to predict the willingness and proficiency of Mathematics Teacher Educators (MTEs) in integrating technology into mathematics instruction. This study employs a machine learning approach to predict the willingness and proficiency of Mathematics Teacher Educators (MTEs) in integrating technology into mathematics instruction. Secondary data from 104 MTEs were analyzed using a decision tree model to identify the most significant predictors of technology integration. The analysis revealed that familiarity with and perceived ease of use of technology were the primary determinants of MTEs' willingness to adopt digital tools in teaching. Moreover, higher education levels and institutional support were associated with greater technological proficiency. Despite limited prior experience, many MTEs displayed a constructive attitude toward technology adoption, suggesting a readiness to engage in continuous digital learning. These findings provide actionable insights for policymakers and professional development designers in developing targeted training programs that enhance digital competence among teacher educators. Beyond its practical implications, this study contributes by showing how machine learning can extend TAM and UTAUT frameworks, revealing nonlinear relationships and offering data-driven insights into technology integration among mathematics teacher educators.

TI Unpacking Philippine Madrasah Education Pedagogies: A Case Study of
   Asatidz' Pedagogical Practices
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ALIVE Program; Asatidz; Madrasah education; Pedagogical practices;
   Philippines
AB The Asatidz, or madrasah teachers, are not necessarily graduates of education courses nor passers of the Philippine Licensure Examination for Teachers. However, they are expected to be adept in both content knowledge, as expressed in the learning competencies of the intended curriculum, and the pedagogical content knowledge needed for the implementation of the instruction. As program implementers, they are expected to perform the tasks of a regular teacher. Thus, this study explored the factors influencing the pedagogical practices of Asatidz in the Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education program in selected schools in Metro Manila. The study was anchored in a case study research model. Data were gathered from ten madrasah teachers through semi-structured individual interviews, classroom observations, and the collection of artifacts. Analysis of the data revealed several salient factors influencing the pedagogical practices of Asatidz: self-efficacy in teaching and learning; Islamic education's conception of traditional teaching methodologies and practices; teacher training in enhancing instructional practices; and mentoring. Based on these findings, the study recommends providing professional development programs for the Asatidz focused on high-quality instruction grounded in their context and needs assessment.

TI Family-School Relationships in Contexts of Social Vulnerability:
   Perspectives from Chilean Teachers
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational parental role; elementary school; qualitative research;
   teachers; vulnerability
AB Existing literature primarily highlights family-school relationships as a key indicator in students' educational development as well as the relevance of family involvement in the school process. However, there remains a gap in research regarding teachers' perspectives and real participation practices in contexts of socially disadvantaged educational contexts. This research aims to explore teachers' views on fulfilling the educational role of parents in contexts of social vulnerability, understood as the varying levels of risk faced by individuals. The study employs a qualitative approach, with data collected through semi-structured individual interviews conducted with twenty-four elementary school teachers from the south-central region of Chile. Data analysis was carried out using the Argumentative Action-Situation Analysis Model. The findings reveal that teachers conceptualize vulnerability from multiple perspectives, but the actions to address it are modelled in a homogeneous and standardized way. In other words, it is conceptualized in plural terms (vulnerabilities), and the actions defined by the school are established homogeneously and singularly (vulnerability). Finally, the study contributes to highlighting the need for more context-responsive family-school relationships, shifting the focus from bureaucratic approaches to equity-oriented educational practices.

TI Employability Skills for Individuals with Autism Spectrum
   Disorder/Intellectual Disabilities: Gaps and Expectations
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE autism; career education; employability; intellectual disabilities;
   Indonesia; postsecondary education
ID EMPLOYMENT
AB Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and/or intellectual disability (ID) in Indonesia face persistent barriers to meaningful employment despite completing postsecondary education (PSE). The absence of structured, inclusive career education tailored to their needs contributes to high rates of unemployment and underemployment among this population. This study aims to identify the employability skill gaps faced by individuals and analyze the expectations of key stakeholders, including parents and employers, regarding career readiness. Using a mixed-method design, this study incorporated a literature review, semi-structured interviews with 23 individuals with ASD, ID, and ASD with ID, and questionnaires completed by 31 stakeholders. Employability skills were analyzed across eight domains inspired by Rosenberg's 46-skills framework. The results indicate that, while individuals show strength in work ethics and interpersonal skills, they experience major deficits in management, systematic thinking, and technology use. Stakeholders emphasize the importance of developing social skills, fostering independence, and gaining exposure to real-world work environments. Self-employment is often chosen out of necessity because of workplace stigma and a lack of support. These findings underscore the urgent need for an inclusive, individualized, skills-based career education curriculum that aligns with the local work culture and socioeconomic contexts. This study provides a foundation for future research and underscored the value of stakeholder-driven approaches to bridge the school-to-work transition gap for individuals with ASD and/or ID in Indonesia.

TI AI-Driven Pedagogical Empowerment in International Education:
   Transforming Teaching Practices for College Faculty Through
   Faculty-Centered Innovation
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence in education; cross-cultural education; faculty
   development; institutional trust; pedagogical autonomy
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE
AB The study examines the contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to the strengthening of faculty potential in global higher education, with focus on pedagogical autonomy, cultural sensitivity and the sense of inclusivity in the respective institutions. A sequential mixed-methods design was used to collect data that was based on the survey of 150 faculty members across Asia, Europe, and North America combined with region-specific focus groups. With the help of UTAUT and Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) frameworks, the study reveals the Institutional Trust and Training and Support Needs as important outlooks of AI adoption and pedagogical empowerment, whereas traditional determinants of adoption, such as Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy became irrelevant unless aligned to specific cultural and institutional contexts. Faculty consider hybrid AI-human models of instruction, cultural responsiveness-based training, and collaborative decision-making. This study differs with those that concentrate on student-oriented AI-related applications in that faculty is positioned as pedagogic constructors. The developed findings will guide universities to adopt AI by implementing faculty-oriented, culturally responsive measures, which will support equitable, ethical, and sustainable innovations in international classrooms.

TI Core Competencies for Inclusive Early Childhood Educators: A Systematic
   Review
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE core competencies for inclusive education; inclusive early childhood
   education; inclusive education training; inclusive teacher competencies
ID TEACHERS COMPETENCES; EXPERIENCE
AB This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) synthesizes findings from 41 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025 to identify the core competencies required for inclusive early childhood educators. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the review employed a structured search across four academic databases and applied thematic synthesis to analyze competency frameworks across diverse educational contexts. Seven competency domains were identified, that is, differentiation and curriculum adaptation, collaborative practice, inclusive knowledge and disability awareness, positive attitudes and inclusive values, assistive and educational technology use, reflective practice, and psychological readiness. The findings demonstrate the interconnectedness of competencies with reflective practice as the fundamental core of teacher competency. Psychological readiness, encompassing emotional resilience and self-identity development, is an under-discussed domain in the existing literature. Competency development in this study is depicted as a recursive and continuous spiral model. This study recommends unifying the previously fragmented literature on inclusive education and emphasizing the emotional and responsive preparation of teachers to various contexts and changes. The review offers implications for curriculum designers, policymakers, and researchers, advocating a shift from short-term technical interventions to long-term, holistic frameworks grounded in justice-oriented pedagogy.

TI Ghana's Standards-Based Curriculum Reform: National Insights from the
   Bono East Region Experience
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE curriculum development; equitable education; education policy reforms;
   standards-based curriculum; teacher preparedness
AB One of the keys to promoting equitable education is implementing a Standards-Based Curriculum; however, understanding the challenges of such implementation is crucial. Ghana progressively undertook this implementation beginning in the 2019-2020 school year. This study explored the perspectives on implementation challenges among district administrators, curriculum trainers, and local teachers in Ghana using Bono East Region as a case study. Bono East is one of the country's most economically disadvantaged areas. The sample consisted of 253 participants from an approximate target population of 300, yielding a response rate of about 84%. A MANOVA revealed a significant multivariate effect of teacher role on the combined indicators of SBC implementation training and resource adequacy-Pillai's Trace = .197, F(4, 492) = 13.42, p < .001, partial eta(2) = .098. However, follow-up univariate tests showed no significant differences in perceived resource adequacy across roles (p > .05), indicating that the variation was driven primarily by differences in training perceptions. The study's potential benefits include guidance for future curriculum rollouts to minimize regional implementation barriers. Though minimal due to anonymity, risks included teacher concerns about revealing incompetence and administrator fears of political backlash for highlighting government funding gaps. These were mitigated through assured anonymity and no political data sharing. The results may inform policies and strategies to improve regional equity and effectiveness in future national curriculum implementations. Further research could examine the relative significance of identified barriers and trial interventions to address them.

TI Evaluating the Socioeconomic Value of Low-Threshold Youth Clubs in the
   Czech Republic: Bridging Data Gaps in Informal Education Through Social
   Return on Investment and Theory of Change
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Czech Republic; econometrics; European Commission; low-threshold clubs;
   social return on investment; theory of change; youth policy
AB This study evaluates the financing and policy architecture of low-threshold clubs for children and youth in the Czech Republic-informal educational spaces that provide preventive, developmental, and integrative services to vulnerable populations. Specifically, the study examines: (a) national-level funding flows and expenditures across five major providers; (b) local operational realities in a case study of & Uacute;sti nad Labem; and (c) the European Commission's policy stance on social infrastructure co-financing. The analysis draws on a semi-synthetic dataset constructed from public financial reports, ministry allocations, and interpolated values based on provider averages. Descriptive statistics and a simple linear regression model (Adj. R2 = .971) demonstrate that approximately 91.2% of total funding is linearly translated into operational expenditures. Additionally, the Social Return on Investment (SROI) framework is applied to map the broader impact of these centres, including volunteer contributions and community outcomes, using a theory-of-change logic model. Results show a heavy reliance on EU operational programmes-particularly OP VVV, which covers an estimated 74% of total funding-with national and local sources unable to compensate for its absence. The fragmented governance across ministries (Education, Social Affairs, Interior, Health) further impedes coordinated data collection and long-term planning. These findings underscore the need for integrated, multi-ministerial policy frameworks, sustained funding cycles, and formal recognition of volunteer and informal educational contributions. The study provides a replicable model for assessing cost-effectiveness and long-term value in youth social services at both national and European levels.

TI Educational Equity at the Geopolitical Frontier A Music-Based Teacher
   Training Case
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; equity; inclusion; music education; open-source
   technologies; teacher training
ID TRANSFORMATION; PERCEPTIONS; PEDAGOGY; ISSUES; AGENCY; MODEL
AB This paper presents a case study of a music-centered professional development program designed to promote educational equity at a geopolitical frontier. Taking place on the island of Lesvos in Greece, a transcontinental threshold shaped by migration, marginalization and resource disparities, the training brought together 36 primary and secondary music teachers to explore creative and inclusive uses of open-source and AI-assisted tools. Grounded in design-based research and guided by A/r/tographic methodology, the session introduced accessible technologies with a focus on AI, music composition, sound editing and ethical media sourcing for educational settings. Activities included hands-on experimentation with diegetic and nondiegetic music and the use of AI-generated soundtracks for school projects. Qualitative data from reflections, digital artefacts and participant feedback reveal increased teacher confidence in integrating digital tools and a stronger awareness of music's role in inclusive pedagogy. Four themes characterized the experience: enhanced creative confidence through low-barrier experimentation, pedagogical imagination in using sound to support belonging and non-verbal expression, ethical and cultural awareness around authorship and representation in AI tools and a collaborative dynamic that reinforced agency through peer dialogue. Teachers highlighted the relevance of these approaches for engaging diverse student populations, particularly in classrooms serving marginalized and culturally diverse learners. This case study shows how focused teacher training can foster inclusive pedagogy and support educational equity in regions shaped by social and geographic isolation. It adds to ongoing conversations about how AI and open-source tools can enrich arts education and suggests that creative, community-rooted professional development has the potential to inspire change in Europe's educational peripheries.

TI The PRIME Framework: A Design-Based, Pace-Sensitive RME Approach for
   Inclusive Mathematics in Indonesia
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE design research; inclusive education; learning pace; realistic
   mathematics education; multi-tiered systems of support; universal design
   for learning
AB This design research study investigates how pace-sensitive and inclusive mathematics instruction can support students who learn at slower, moderate, and faster paces in Indonesian junior high classrooms. Using the PRIME framework-Profiling, Reconstruction, Implementation, Measurement, and Engagement-the study was implemented across two iterative cycles in two comparable inclusive classes (N = 80, Grade 8). Each cycle employed contextual mathematical tasks integrating local and global themes, such as fishing tides, travel-based time zones, temperature changes, skyscraper scaling, and communal food sharing, all grounded in Realistic Mathematics Education (RME). Students' learning-pace profiles were established through triangulated diagnostics including cognitive screening instruments, self-assessment, teacher interviews, and Level 0 contextual tasks. Within each cycle, descriptive analyses indicated clear improvements in students' representational clarity, strategic reasoning, and movement through the RME phases, particularly among students who initially struggled with abstraction. Cycle 2 demonstrated more substantial gains than Cycle 1, with students exhibiting increased independence, reduced need for teacher prompting, and stronger transitions from model-of to model-for reasoning. Qualitative thematic analysis further showed enhanced engagement, contextual understanding, and confidence, while teachers reported more manageable routines for differentiation. The findings suggest that learning pace is malleable and responsive to purposeful instructional design. The PRIME framework offers a practical bridge between RME, differentiated instruction, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS), providing a feasible model for promoting equitable mathematics learning in resource-variable inclusive classrooms.

TI Professional Development of EFL Instructors in Indonesia: Challenges
   from Higher Education Institutions
SO IAFOR JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE English language instructors; higher education institutions; MAXQDA;
   qualitative research; professional development
ID ENGLISH; TEACHERS; UNIVERSITIES
AB This qualitative study investigates the professional development challenges faced by English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instructors in Indonesian higher education. Based on a reflexive thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews conducted with ten instructors from five different universities, and utilising MAXQDA for data management, this study discovers four interconnected themes: limited access to pedagogical resources, institutional constraints, workload pressures, and personal limitations. Participants reported difficulties in accessing current ELT knowledge, particularly in remote areas, and highlighted the impact of rigid institutional structures, accreditation requirements and seniority-based promotion systems on PD engagement. Gendered responsibilities and family obligations, particularly among female teachers, have further restricted participation in long-term PD programmes. These results confirm and complicate the existing literature on PD in Southeast Asia and reveal how systemic, cultural and logistical factors intersect to shape the professional development of instructors. The study highlights the need for more comprehensive and context-sensitive PD policies, including digital resource platforms, flexible timetables, and family support systems. It also calls for institutional reforms to prioritize pedagogical quality rather than bureaucratic compliance. To tackle these issues, institutions of higher education should establish organised mentoring initiatives and dedicate specific time for the development of instructors.

TI Students' readiness for learner autonomy: A comparative analysis of EFL
   learning in French and Algerian universities
SO RECHERCHE ET PRATIQUES PEDAGOGIQUES EN LANGUES DE SPECIALITE-CAHIERS DE
   L APLIUT
LA English
DT Article
DE autonomy; English as a foreign language; learning strategies; teaching
   strategies; university
ID EMPOWERMENT
AB The present study examines language learner autonomy in first-year undergraduate English majors in France and Algeria. As a concept closely related to empowerment, autonomy is a complex learning variable, pertaining to one's capacity for reflection and goal setting. Despite its highly personalized nature, learner autonomy can be influenced by a variety of factors including local culture, teachers, peers, and learning material. While the advantages of having autonomous learning skills are well-established, many students struggle to take charge of their learning. This study, therefore, aims at investigating this phenomenon. It uses an adapted version of the Learner Autonomy Readiness Questionnaire by Kartal and Bal & ccedil;ikanli (2019) to collect data from two universities in France and Algeria. Results show that while students from both countries demonstrate some degree of ownership over their learning, they still tend to rely on teachers for making decisions, particularly among Algerian students. Possible reasons for these results are discussed along with directions for future research.

TI Empowering university EFL learners through peer review
SO RECHERCHE ET PRATIQUES PEDAGOGIQUES EN LANGUES DE SPECIALITE-CAHIERS DE
   L APLIUT
LA English
DT Article
DE checklist; Eval+ project; mirror effect; peer review; peer-to-peer
   assessment; positive assessment
ID FEEDBACK
AB This study focuses on a teaching practice intended to empower students and support their success; namely peer review (Woodward, 2015; Massery, 2013). Here, peer review is implemented with a group of 16 third-year French-speaking undergraduate students enrolled in an English studies programme. We hypothesize that a peer review process prior to the final evaluation (a ten-minute oral presentation with a slideshow) serves to enhance students' understanding of the assessment criteria (made explicit through the use of a checklist) and contributes to improving the quality of their initial work. The results show that: (i) students tend to underrate their own productions and overrate those of their partners; (ii) they integrate more assessment criteria and revise their work accordingly; (iii) their second self-evaluation procedure aligns more closely with the teacher's final evaluation procedure; (iv) they report experiencing a "mirror effect" in the way they revise their work.

TI Effects of teachers' interpersonal style on the self-presentation on
   social media by secondary school physical education students: the
   mediating role of positive and negative affect
SO REVISTA PUBLICACIONES
LA English
DT Article
DE autonomy support; controlling; self-determination theory; ideal-self;
   false-self; real-self
ID FIT INDEXES; MOTIVATIONAL CLIMATE; MODEL; QUESTIONNAIRE; SENSITIVITY;
   STRATEGIES; REAL
AB Introduction: Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the present study examines the ef-fects of perceived teaching styles (autonomy-supportive and controlling) on adolescents' self-presentation on social media, mediated by positive and negative affect. Method: This cross-sectional study involved 2,438 secondary-school Physical Education stu-dents (Mage = 16.15, SD = 2.01). Teacher interpersonal style was assessed as autonomy support and controlling style, and self-presentation on social media was operationalized through real self, ideal self, self-exploration, false self-deception, false self-comparison, and false self-exploration. Results: Structural equation modeling (SEM) revealed that an autonomy-supportive teach-ing style was positively associated with positive affect, whereas a controlling style predict-ed higher levels of negative affect. In turn, positive affect was related to more adaptive self-perceptions, reflected in online presentations of the real self, the ideal self, and self-ex-ploration (i.e., the display of different facets of one's identity). Conversely, negative affect was associated with maladaptive forms of online self-presentation, namely false self-de-ception, false self-comparison, and false self-exploration as well as with lower perceptions of the real self. Significant indirect effects supported the mediating role of affect in the relationship between teaching styles and self-presentation on social media. Conclusions: These findings underscore the importance of fostering emotionally safe class-room climates and autonomy-supportive teaching as a means to promote positive affective experiences and contribute to the development of a more adaptive personal identity during adolescence.

TI Participation of Special Olympics Athletes in the USA Games Step
   Challenge
SO PALAESTRA
LA English
DT Article
DE and developmental disabilities; wearable activity; monitoring; Special
   Olympics programming
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES; ADULTS; HEALTH;
   INTERVENTION; TECHNOLOGY; OVERWEIGHT; OBESITY; PEOPLE; LIFE
AB Adults with intellectual disabilities have low physical activity levels, increasing chronic health risks. Special Olympics promotes health through education and programming. This project evaluated the Road to the USA Games Step Challenge, a 20-week nationwide program aiming for 1 million steps using FitbitTM monitors and the SO FitNow app. The app tracked progress, provided education, fostered social support, and facilitated goal setting. Athletes from all 50 states participated; 36.1% achieved the goal, with males outperforming females in step count (p = 0.019). Median daily steps increased significantly, though participation declined to 60.8% by Week 20 (p < 0.001). This large-scale program demonstrated feasibility through engagement across all 50 states, significant step count improvements, and successful goal achievement for many participants, offering insights for future programming.

TI A Bibliometric Dive into Goalball Studies
SO PALAESTRA
LA English
DT Article
DE Bibliometric analysis; Paralympic Games; physical fitness; thematic
   analysis; visual impairment
ID PHYSICAL-FITNESS
AB Goalball is sport that has the high potential to positively influence the lives of visually impaired people. This research used Bibliometrix, an R package for bibliometric analysis. Bibliometric studies are used in many global studies and analysis of research trends. A database search was conducted on the Web of Science (WoS) to identify articles related to Goalball. This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of Goalball research from 2004 to 2024 to chart key developments and trends in the field. According to the most important keywords in this area, it has focused on concepts such as Goalball, visually impaired people, and Paralympic Games. Also, motor themes like performance analysis, match analysis, and Paralympics sport are among the prominent findings of this section, highlight their pivotal role in advancing theoretical understanding and practical applications in the field. These results help to strengthen the scientific understanding and practical applications of Goalball. Data analysis related to global trends, leading authors, and institutions in this field indicates increased scientific attention to the Paralympic sport of Goalball.

TI Hosting a Paralympic Festival with Your College Students: Training the
   Next Generation to Lead
SO PALAESTRA
LA English
DT Article
DE Disability sport; inclusion; awareness; Ableism; higher education;
   Paralympics sports
ID SCHOOL DAY; PHYSICAL-EDUCATION; INTERVENTION PROGRAM; INCLUSION;
   ATTITUDES; DISABILITY; CHILDREN
AB Over the years there have been several models of Paralympic Sport programming and Disabilities awareness program within Physical Education contexts for a variety of age levels. These include the Paralympic Sports Day (PSD) for youth in K-12 settings, the Paralympic Sports Lab (PSL) for college students, and Inclusive Sports at School (ISS) for college students. Mainly, the programs aim to develop knowledge of Paralympic sports and change the attitudes of people without disabilities towards Paralympic athletes and sports through an immersive experience. Since the first guidelines published in 2006 by the International Paralympic Committee, several studies have highlighted the attitude change of the participants who engaged in these Paralympic experiences. The purpose of this article is to provide another option for a Paralympic sports program that trains future teachers to lead. The purpose, process, and specific program structure are provided so the reader can replicate this innovative program.

TI Enhancing Community Instructors' Skills in Inclusive Exercise through
   Online Training
SO PALAESTRA
LA English
DT Article
DE Physical activity; online training; self-efficacy; professional
   development
ID EDUCATION; PEOPLE; DISABILITIES; FACILITIES; PROGRAM
AB Individuals with disabilities (IWD) participate in community-based exercise programs at lower rates than non-disabled individuals, partly due to a lack of trained wellness instructors. The Strategies of Success (SOS) online modules were developed to address knowledge and self-efficacy gaps in inclusive programming. This study examined their impact on 830 wellness instructors, educators, and professionals. Results showed significant knowledge improvement (Cohen's d > 1.4), with 72% reporting increased self-efficacy. Online training is a cost-effective way to enhance instructor preparedness, though organizational support remains crucial. SOS modules serve as a valuable professional development tool for promoting inclusive physical activity programs.
